east-indies: European exploration of the region began in the last three years of the 15th century and continued into the 16th, led by Portuguese explorers after the Cape Route had been found. The Portuguese called the whole region they reached the Indies. Christopher Columbus, who had grossly underestimated the westward distance from Europe to Asia, at first took the New World for the easternmost part of the Indies. To avoid confusion the Americas came to be called the West Indies, also the New Indies or Little Indies, and the original Indies the East Indies, also the Old Indies or Great Indies.

The term has had a broad and a narrow sense. In the Age of Discovery it covered the coasts of the Indian subcontinent and the Indochinese Peninsula together with the Malay Archipelago. In the narrow sense it meant the Malay Archipelago alone, which today comprises the Indonesian Archipelago, New Guinea and the Philippine Archipelago. The former Dutch New Guinea, however, is geographically counted as part of Melanesia and is not included.

Parts of the region are sometimes named after the colonial empire that held them. The Spanish East Indies, the Philippines, were Spanish territory for 333 years before the American conquest and later independence. The Dutch East Indies kept that name for about 300 years until Indonesian independence, and British East Indies refers to Malaysia. The term may also take in the former French Indochina, the former British territories of Brunei, Hong Kong and Singapore, and the former Portuguese Macau and Timor.

The peoples of the region are culturally very diverse and do not consider themselves a single ethnic group. Most are Austronesians, whose ancestors first expanded from the island of Taiwan. In the early modern period Han Chinese began to migrate south and became known as the Peranakans or Straits Chinese. Buddhism, Christianity, Islam and Hinduism are the most widespread religions.

After the founding of European trading companies in the 17th century, among them the British East India Company and the Dutch East India Company, the Indies were important sources of trade goods, particularly cotton, indigo and spices. The name East Indian was once applied to people of all the East Indies, to keep them apart from the indigenous peoples of the Americas, who were then simply called Indians. In colonial times South-East Asians who were not from India were also called Indians. Today the inhabitants of the region are not called East Indians.
east-karelia: East Karelia, also called Eastern or Russian Karelia, is the part of Karelia beyond the eastern border of Finland which, since the Treaty of Stolbovo in 1617, has remained Eastern Orthodox and a part of Russia. It is distinguished from the western part, Finnish Karelia, which before 1808 was Swedish Karelia. It consists mainly of two old historical regions, Viena or White Karelia and Aunus or Olonets Karelia.

The Fennomans, ethnic nationalists of the 19th century, saw East Karelia as the ancient home of Finnic culture, untouched by Scandinavians or Slavs. In its sparsely populated backwoods, mainly in White Karelia, Elias Lönnrot (1802–1884) collected the folk tales that became the Kalevala, published from 1835 to 1849. The idea of joining the region to a Greater Finland had wide support in newly independent Finland after 1917.

When Finland and Soviet Russia divided Karelia between them in 1920, the Soviet authorities promised far-reaching cultural rights to the Finnic peoples who made up most of East Karelia's population. Within the Karelian Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic these rights were never realised, and under Stalin ethnic Finns were persecuted and an intensive programme of Russification began.

Annexation was most popular during the Continuation War of 1941–1944, when an expected German conquest of the Soviet Union made it seem feasible. Finnish forces occupied most of East Karelia from 1941 to 1944, and the war brought hardship to the local ethnic Russian civilians, including forced labour and internment in prison camps as enemy aliens. After the Moscow Armistice of September 1944 calls for annexation virtually disappeared.

Most of East Karelia is now part of the Republic of Karelia within the Russian Federation. Since the dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991, Finnic culture in the region has experienced a revival. In Finnish the region is called Itä-Karjala or Venäjän Karjala, and in Karelian Idä-Karjala.
ecomog: The members of the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) agreed a Protocol on Mutual Defence Assistance at Freetown on 29 May 1981, which provided for an allied armed force when needed. ECOMOG itself was created by the Standing Mediation Committee at its meeting in Banjul on 6 and 7 August 1990. The Nigerian scholar Adekeye Adebajo has written that this body stood on shaky legal foundations, that the guidelines of the defence protocol were not followed, and that the force was justified largely on humanitarian grounds.

It was the English-speaking members of ECOWAS that acted, intervening in the Liberian civil war that had begun in 1989. Several French-speaking members strongly opposed the deployment, and the leaders of Burkina Faso and Côte d'Ivoire supported Charles Taylor in his attempt to depose Samuel Doe.

Unlike the usual United Nations mission of the time, the force had to fight its way into a many-sided civil war to hold the factions apart. Most of its men and resources came from the Nigerian Armed Forces, with smaller units from Ghana, Guinea, Sierra Leone, The Gambia and others. Its first commander was the Ghanaian Lieutenant General Arnold Quainoo; after Samuel Doe was killed by Prince Johnson's Independent National Patriotic Front of Liberia on 9 September 1990, Major General Joshua Dogonyaro took over, the first of an unbroken line of Nigerian commanders.

Senegal sent 1,500 soldiers with some financial support from the United States, but withdrew them all by mid-January 1993, after six were killed in a confrontation with Taylor's supporters at Vahun on 28 May 1992. Corruption and organised looting by its troops led some Liberians to read the acronym as Every Car or Movable Object Gone. After Taylor was elected president on 19 July 1997, the last field commander, General Timothy Shelpidi, withdrew the force fully by the end of 1998.

Within Africa the force was the first credible attempt at a regional security initiative since the Organisation of African Unity tried to send an Inter-African Force to Chad in 1981. A deployment of 1,700 men planned in 2001 for the border between Guinea and Liberia never took place, for lack of funds and because of fighting in Liberia. In 2003, under pressure from the United States, ECOWAS launched a similar mission, ECOMIL, to halt the rebel occupation of Monrovia during the Second Liberian Civil War; it was soon succeeded by the United Nations mission UNMIL.
edirne: Edirne lies in the northwestern part of the province of Edirne in Eastern Thrace, 7 km from the Greek border and 20 km from the Bulgarian border. Its position in the border region between Asia and Europe gave rise to the claim that it is the most frequently contested spot on earth. The through highway that connects Europe to Istanbul, Anatolia and the Middle East passes through it, and the surrounding lowlands are productive farmland.

The city was founded on an earlier Thracian settlement. A Greek city, Orestias, stood on the site, and the Roman emperor Hadrian re-established it, adorned it with monuments and renamed it Hadrianopolis, anglicised as Adrianople. Constantine I defeated Licinius there in 324, and the Emperor Valens was killed by the Goths at the Battle of Adrianople in 378. After the Byzantine defeat at the Battle of Versinikia in 813, Khan Krum of Bulgaria seized the city and moved its inhabitants to the Bulgarian lands north of the Danube. In 1077 Nikephoros Bryennios rebelled there against Emperor Michael VII Doukas.

In the period of the Latin Empire of Constantinople, the Bulgarian Emperor Kaloyan defeated the Crusaders at the Battle of Adrianople in 1205. The Latin regime gave the city to the Byzantine aristocrat Theodore Branas as a hereditary fief in 1206, and Theodore Komnenos, Despot of Epirus, took it in 1227. In 1321 Andronikos III made it his base for the First Palaiologan civil war against his grandfather, Emperor Andronikos II.

The city fell to the Ottomans around 1369. Its church declined, its properties were confiscated and its Metropolitan was taken prisoner and died in captivity. A document of 1389 states that the new Metropolitan could not enter the city and had to carry out his duties from Constantinople. Edirne was the second capital of the Ottoman Empire from the 1360s to 1453.

Edirne is the seat of Edirne Province and a commercial centre for woven textiles, silks, carpets and agricultural products. The Selimiye Mosque, built in 1575 to the design of Mimar Sinan for Sultan Selim II, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2011. Two earlier mosques also stand in the centre: the Eski Cami, begun in 1403 and finished in 1422, and the Üç Şerefli Mosque, built between 1437 and 1447 for Sultan Murad II. The Kırkpınar oil-wrestling tournament, held each year in late June or early July, was inscribed on UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage in 2010.
egypt: Egypt spans the northeast corner of Africa and the southwest corner of Asia through the Sinai Peninsula, and covers 1,001,450 square kilometres. The climate is extremely arid, so population centres are concentrated along the narrow Nile Valley and Delta: about 98% of Egyptians live on 3% of the territory.

Apart from the Nile Valley the landscape is mostly desert, with a few oases such as Siwa, and parts of the Sahara and the Libyan Desert fall within it. Mount Catherine, at 2,642 metres on the Sinai Peninsula, is the highest mountain. The Suez Canal crosses the Isthmus of Suez and connects the Mediterranean Sea with the Indian Ocean by way of the Red Sea.

Evidence of rock carvings along the Nile and in the oases indicates early habitation. By about 6000 BCE a Neolithic culture had taken root in the Nile Valley, and the earliest known hieroglyphic inscriptions appeared on Naqada III pottery vessels dated to about 3200 BCE. Around c. 3150 BCE King Menes unified Egypt, establishing a succession of dynasties that ruled for three millennia.

The Old Kingdom (c. 2700 to 2200 BCE) saw the construction of the pyramids at Giza, and Ahmose I reunified the country after the Hyksos occupation, founding the Eighteenth Dynasty and the New Kingdom (c. 1550 to 1070 BCE). Its pharaohs included Hatshepsut, Thutmose III, Akhenaten, Tutankhamun and Ramesses II.

Egypt came under foreign rule from the 6th century BCE. It was an early centre of Christianity and adopted Islam from the seventh century onwards. Cairo became the capital of the Fatimid Caliphate in the tenth century and of the Mamluk Sultanate in the 13th century, and Egypt became part of the Ottoman Empire in 1517.

Muhammad Ali established modern Egypt as an autonomous Khedivate in 1867. The country was then occupied by the British Empire and gained independence in 1922 as a monarchy, and after the 1952 revolution it declared itself a republic. Egypt signed the Camp David Accords in 1978, and the Sinai Peninsula was completely returned to it in 1982.

Egypt is the most populous country in the Arab world, with about 120 million inhabitants, and Cairo is its capital and largest city. The 2011 revolution overthrew Hosni Mubarak. Islam is the official religion and Arabic the official language.
elizabeth-ii: Elizabeth was born at 2:40 am on 21 April 1926 at 17 Bruton Street in Mayfair, London, the first child of Prince Albert, Duke of York, later King George VI, and Elizabeth, Duchess of York, later Queen Elizabeth the Queen Mother. She was third in line to the throne behind her uncle Edward, Prince of Wales, and her father, but was not expected to become queen. Her sister, Princess Margaret, was born in 1930, and the two were educated at home, with lessons in history, language, literature and music.

On 6 February 1952 Elizabeth, aged 25, was in Kenya on the way to a tour of Australia and New Zealand when word came of her father's death. She kept Elizabeth as her regnal name and was proclaimed queen throughout her realms, becoming queen of seven independent Commonwealth countries and head of the Commonwealth. On 9 April 1952 she declared that the royal house would remain Windsor, though Philip had hoped for his own name. In 1960 the surname Mountbatten-Windsor was adopted for those of their male-line descendants who bear no royal titles.

She reigned as a constitutional monarch through the decolonisation of Africa, the Troubles in Northern Ireland, devolution in the United Kingdom, and its accession to the European Communities and later withdrawal. The number of her realms varied as territories gained independence and most realms became republics. She was advised by more than 170 prime ministers across her realms, and her events included her coronation in 1953 and the Silver, Golden, Diamond and Platinum jubilees. She made state visits to China in 1986, to Russia in 1994 and to the Republic of Ireland in 2011.

Elizabeth died at Balmoral Castle in Scotland at 3:10 pm on 8 September 2022, aged 96, and was succeeded by her eldest son, Charles III. She was the first monarch to die in Scotland since James V in 1542. Her coffin lay at St Giles' Cathedral in Edinburgh and then in Westminster Hall, where an estimated 250,000 people filed past. Her state funeral was held at Westminster Abbey on 19 September, the first monarch's funeral service there since that of George II in 1760, and she was interred at Windsor with her husband Philip.
england: England covers about 62 per cent of the island of Great Britain, together with more than 100 smaller islands, among them the Isle of Wight and the Isles of Scilly. It shares land borders with Scotland to the north and Wales to the west. Most of the landscape is low hills and plains, with uplands in the north and west, including the Pennines, the Lake District and the Cheviot Hills. The highest point is Scafell Pike, at 978 metres. The Severn, at 350 kilometres, is the longest river flowing through England, and the Thames, at 346 kilometres, the longest entirely within it.

The earliest evidence of human presence is that of Homo antecessor, about 780,000 years ago. Humans repopulated the area roughly 11,000 years ago as the ice sheets receded, and Neolithic farmers from the Iberian Peninsula arrived around 4100 BCE. The Beaker culture, from around 2,500 BCE, brought clay vessels and bronze, and monuments such as Stonehenge and Avebury date from this time. The Romans founded the first cities and towns, among them London, Bath, York, Chester and St Albans, and built Hadrian's Wall across the north.

The name England comes from the Old English Englaland, the land of the Angles, a Germanic people who settled in the 5th and 6th centuries. The earliest recorded use, as Engla londe, is in a late-ninth-century Old English translation of Bede's Ecclesiastical History of the English People. England became a unified state in the 10th century.

After the Norman conquest of 1066 castles such as the Tower of London and Windsor Castle were built, and the University of Oxford was founded in 1096 and the University of Cambridge in 1209. The Kingdom of England, which included Wales after 1535, ceased to be a separate sovereign state on 1 May 1707 under the Acts of Union.

England is governed directly by the Parliament of the United Kingdom and has no devolved parliament of its own, unlike Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. A plan for regional devolution was dropped after the North East rejected it in a 2004 referendum. The population was 56,490,048 in the 2021 census, about 84 per cent of the United Kingdom's, with London as the largest city.

The Industrial Revolution began in 18th-century England, which became the first industrialised nation. The English language, the English legal system and association football originated there, and its parliamentary system has been widely adopted by other nations. The Bank of England was founded in 1694, and the National Health Service began on 5 July 1948, based on the Beveridge Report.
english-language: English is a West Germanic language of the Indo-European family that emerged in early medieval England. It is named after the Angles, one of the Germanic peoples who migrated to Britain after the end of Roman rule. Old English developed from West Germanic dialects originally spoken along the coasts of Frisia, Lower Saxony and southern Jutland by the Angles, Saxons and Jutes. It was spoken from c. 450 to c. 1150. From the 5th century the Anglo-Saxons settled Britain as the Roman economy and administration collapsed, and by the 7th century Old English had become dominant, replacing the Common Brittonic and British Latin previously spoken.

Old English was divided into two Anglian dialects, Mercian and Northumbrian, and two Saxon dialects, Kentish and West Saxon. Through the influence of the kingdom of Wessex and the educational reforms of King Alfred in the 9th century, West Saxon became the standard written variety, and the epic poem Beowulf is written in it. Early inscriptions used runes, and by the 7th century a Latin alphabet had been adopted.

Late Old English borrowed some grammar and core vocabulary from Old Norse. Middle English emerged in England under Norman control and borrowed vocabulary extensively from French dialects, the source of approximately 28 per cent of Modern English words, and from Latin, the source of another 28 per cent. Middle English then transformed, in part through the Great Vowel Shift, into Modern English. Speakers of the 21st century cannot understand Old English without special training.

English is the most spoken language in the world, primarily because of the global influence of the British Empire and the rise of the United States, though it is only the third-most spoken native language, after Mandarin Chinese and Spanish. It is the official language, or one of the official languages, of 57 sovereign states and 30 dependent territories. It is a co-official language of the United Nations and the European Union, and the de facto lingua franca of diplomacy, science, technology and international trade. Its grammar and phonology remain Germanic, as does most of its everyday vocabulary.
eritrea: Eritrea lies between latitudes 12° and 18°N on the Red Sea, with a total area of approximately 117,600 square kilometres that includes the Dahlak Archipelago and several of the Hanish Islands. A branch of the East African Rift bisects the country. A hot, arid coastal plain gives way to cooler and more fertile highlands that reach up to 3,000 metres and are a northern extension of the Ethiopian Highlands. The highest point is Emba Soira, at 3,018 metres.

Fossil remains known as Madam Buya, found at an Eritrean site by Italian anthropologists, have been dated to 1 million years old. Tools from the Barka Valley dating from 8,000 BCE appear to give the first concrete evidence of settlement, and excavations near Agordat found the pre-Aksumite Gash Group, with ceramics dated to between 2,500 and 1,500 BCE. Parts of Eritrea were likely part of the Land of Punt around 2,000 BCE, known from Egyptian records of trade expeditions.

The Kingdom of Aksum, centred in Eritrea and northern Ethiopia, was established in the first or second century CE, and the Persian prophet Mani considered it one of the four great powers of the world. It adopted Christianity around the middle of the fourth century. From the 12th century the Zagwe and Solomonid dynasties held fluctuating control over the plateau and the Red Sea coast. In the 16th century the Ottomans failed to conquer the Ethiopian Highlands and were limited to the Eritrean coastline.

The coast came under the Khedivate of Egypt in May 1865 and passed to Italy in February 1885, and Italian Eritrea was formed in 1889. After British administration from 1942, Eritrea federated with Ethiopia under a UN decision of 1952, and Ethiopia annexed it in 1962. Eritrea won de facto independence in 1991 and de jure independence in 1993 after a referendum.

Asmara is the capital and largest city. The name Eritrea derives from the Greek name for the Red Sea, the Erythraean Sea, and was formally adopted in 1890. The country has nine recognised ethnic groups, each with a distinct language, and Tigrinya is the most widely spoken. Most people are Christian or Muslim. On 8 July 2017 the entire city of Asmara, with its Art Deco, futurist and modernist buildings from the Italian period, was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
esen-taishi: Esen was the son of Toghon, the Oirat taishi, of the Choros clan. The title, derived from a Chinese term, was the highest rank among the Mongols below that of khan, which Toghon could not hold because he was not of the lineage of Genghis Khan. In the 1420s Esen led three successful campaigns against Eastern Moghulistan, twice capturing its ruler Uwais Khan. In the 1430s he fought beside his father against the Khalkha taishi Arughtai, who died in 1434. Toghon then installed Taisun as a puppet Great Khan of the Northern Yuan and married him to Esen's elder sister.

After Toghon died in 1438 Esen inherited his title. In 1443 and again in 1445 Oirats attacked Hami, an oasis that acknowledged Ming suzerainty, and its prince came to the Oirat camp in 1448. In 1445 Esen forced the leaders of the Shazhou and Qizhin guards in western Gansu to accept Mongol titles. By 1447 he had conquered two of the three Uriankhai guards and driven the third to migrate, giving him control from present-day Xinjiang to Korea.

Oirat tributary missions to Beijing, in fact commercial, grew from around a hundred men to more than two thousand. In 1448 a mission falsely claimed over three thousand members and was granted one fifth of the gifts it demanded; the court then rejected a marriage between Esen's son and the imperial family that Chinese interpreters had promised without authority. In July 1449 Esen invaded. Emperor Yingzong of Ming led an army reportedly of half a million men, which was massacred at the Tumu postal station on 1 September. Esen besieged Beijing from 27 to 30 October but withdrew, and in September 1450 the emperor was taken back to China.

Esen and Taisun fell out over the choice of Taisun's successor. Taisun allied with the Ming and with Esen's subordinate Alag, but his brother Agbarjin defected to the Oirats in the winter of 1451. Esen defeated Taisun, who fled and was killed by a local chieftain in early 1452. Esen proclaimed Agbarjin khan and soon murdered him. In a letter of 1453 to the Ming court he styled himself Tian-sheng Khagan of the Great Yuan.

Chinese accounts attribute the revolt against him to his lavish living and heavy drinking. He had also refused the title of taishi to Alag, granting it to his own son Amasanj. Esen was defeated and was killed by a man named Bukun, whose father he had ordered put to death, and the Oirat state collapsed.
esperanto: Before Esperanto, Johann Martin Schleyer (1831–1912) had created Volapük as a neutral universal second language. His movement gained widespread and active use in the 19th century, which showed there was demand for such a language. When the Volapük movement collapsed from within, many of its speakers joined the Esperanto movement, which was linguistically simpler and lacked central control, and many former Volapük clubs became Esperanto clubs.

L. L. Zamenhof, a Jewish ophthalmologist from Białystok, then part of the Russian Empire, created Esperanto in the late 1870s and early 1880s. After several earlier versions, he self-published the first book of grammar, the Unua Libro, on 26 July 1887, under the pseudonym Doktoro Esperanto, 'one who hopes'. He called the language simply the international language. Early speakers grew fond of the pseudonym and began to use it as the name of the language. Besides his native Yiddish and Russian, Zamenhof studied German, Hebrew, Latin, English, Spanish, Lithuanian, Italian, French, Aramaic and Volapük.

The language sits between naturalistic constructed languages, which imitate existing ones, and a priori ones. About 80% of its vocabulary derives from Romance languages, and the remainder chiefly from Germanic, Greek and Slavic languages. New words are formed through extensive use of prefixes, suffixes and compounds, so a smaller set of words can express a great deal. Its default word order is subject–verb–object, and adjectives may stand before or after their nouns. One 2010 typological study concluded that Esperanto is somewhat European in character, but considerably less so than the European languages themselves.

The Universal Esperanto Association has a consultative relationship with the United Nations and UNESCO, which recognised Esperanto as a medium for international understanding in 1954. The League of Nations tried to promote its teaching in member countries, but the resolutions were defeated, mainly by French delegates who saw no need for it. No country has officially adopted it. It has entered the education systems of Hungary and China, and Eötvös Loránd University in Budapest had a department of Interlinguistics and Esperanto from 1966 to 2004.

Esperanto has an estimated 2,000 native speakers and, by two estimates, around 100,000 users. Reform proposals began with Zamenhof's own in 1894 and with Ido in 1907, and several later constructed languages were based on it. Poland added Esperanto to its list of intangible cultural heritage in 2014.
estonia: Estonia lies in the Baltic region of Northern Europe, bordered by the Gulf of Finland to the north, the Baltic Sea to the west, Latvia to the south and Russia to the east. Its territory covers 45,335 square kilometres and includes the mainland, the larger islands of Saaremaa and Hiiumaa, and over 2,300 other islands and islets. Its indented coastline stretches for 3,794 kilometres and is notable for the limestone cliffs of the north coast.

The terrain is generally flat, with an average elevation of about 50 metres. The highest peak, Suur Munamägi in the Haanja Upland, reaches 318 metres. Bogs and mires cover 23.2% of the land, and there are over 1,560 natural lakes, the largest being Lake Peipus on the border with Russia.

The oldest known settlement is Pulli, on the banks of the Pärnu, dating to the early 9th millennium BCE. The Kunda culture is linked to the earliest human habitation in the Mesolithic, and ceramics of the Narva culture appear around 5300 BCE. The Bronze Age began around 1800 BCE and saw the first hill fort settlements, and the Iron Age began around 500 BCE. The name Estonia has been connected to the Aesti, a people first mentioned by the Roman historian Tacitus around 98 CE, though historians differ on whom he meant.

Scandinavian sagas describe the early 7th century defeat and killing of Ingvar Harra, King of the Swedes, by Estonian Vikings. In about 1030 Grand Prince Yaroslav the Wise of Kievan Rus' captured Tartu, and the Sosols destroyed this foothold in 1061. Estonians from the island of Saaremaa, known as Oeselians, joined seaborne raids, and in 1187 Oeselians, Curonians or Karelians sacked Sigtuna, then a major city of Sweden. The indigenous population was one of the last pagan civilisations in Europe to adopt Christianity, after the Northern Crusades of the 13th century.

Estonia is a unitary parliamentary republic. The 101-member Riigikogu is elected for four years, and the president is chosen by the Riigikogu or an electoral college. In 2005 Estonia became the first country to introduce nationwide binding internet voting in local elections. It adopted the euro on 1 January 2011.

The population is nearly 1.4 million. Ethnic Estonians were 88% of the population before World War II, dropped to 61% by 1989 under Soviet immigration, deportations and executions, and rose to 69% by 2006. The Estonian Cultural Autonomy law of 1925 was unique in Europe at the time.
eswatini: Eswatini is a small landlocked kingdom of 17,364 square kilometres, no more than 200 km from north to south and 130 km from east to west, the second smallest country in continental Africa. It is bordered by South Africa on the north, west and south and by Mozambique on the east, where the Lebombo Mountains rise to about 600 m. Four regions run from north to south by elevation: the Highveld, the Middleveld, the Lowveld and the Lubombo plateau. The capital Mbabane is on the Highveld, and Manzini, the main commercial and industrial city, is in the Middleveld.

Artefacts show human activity from the Early Stone Age, around 200,000 years ago. The earliest known inhabitants were Khoisan hunter-gatherers, who were largely replaced by Nguni speakers during the Bantu migrations. Agriculture and iron use date from about the 4th century. The Swazi trace their origins to the Embo-Dlamini, a branch of the Embo-Nguni who settled near Delagoa Bay in Mozambique, where the Embo were a small chiefdom led by Chief Langa.

The Swazis established their kingdom in the mid-18th century under Ngwane III. The country and its people take their name from Mswati II, the 19th-century king under whom the kingdom was expanded and unified. Its boundaries were drawn in 1881 during the European Scramble for Africa. After the Second Boer War the kingdom, as Swaziland, was a British high commission territory from 1903 until it regained full independence on 6 September 1968. In April 2018 the king changed the official name to the Kingdom of Eswatini, the name commonly used in the Swazi language.

Eswatini is an absolute monarchy under a constitution adopted in 2005, with Mbabane as executive capital and Lobamba as legislative capital. Its head of state is the king, or ngwenyama, meaning lion, who by tradition reigns with his mother, the ndlovukati, or she-elephant. SiSwati and English are the official languages, and most people are ethnic Swazi. The traditional homestead centres on a cattle byre, which has ritual as well as practical meaning as a store of wealth and a symbol of prestige.
ethiopia: Ethiopia is a landlocked country in the Horn of Africa, covering 1,104,300 square kilometres. Within it is a vast highland complex of mountains and dissected plateaus, divided by the Great Rift Valley and surrounded by lowlands, steppes or semi-desert. The Ethiopian Highlands are the largest continuous mountain ranges in Africa, and Lake Tana in the north is the source of the Blue Nile.

The terrain ranges from deserts along the eastern border to tropical forests in the south and extensive Afromontane areas in the north and southwest. The country includes Dallol, described as the world's hottest settlement. Endemic species include the gelada, the walia ibex and the Ethiopian wolf. Ethiopia has the second-largest number of UNESCO World Heritage Sites in Africa.

Ethiopia is regarded as one of the earliest sites of anatomically modern humans. The Omo remains, excavated in the southwest, are dated to around 200,000 years ago, and Omo-Kibish I is the oldest anatomically modern Homo sapiens skeleton currently known. The hominid Lucy, Australopithecus afarensis, found in the Awash Valley in 1974, is estimated to have lived 3.2 million years ago. A 30,000-year-old rock shelter at Fincha Habera in the Bale Mountains, at 3,469 metres, is the earliest known permanent human occupation at high altitude.

The Kingdom of D'mt extended over Eritrea and northern Ethiopia from about 980 BCE, and the Kingdom of Aksum maintained a unified civilisation for 900 years; Christianity arrived there in 330 CE. After Aksum collapsed in 960, the Zagwe dynasty ruled the north-central region until Yekuno Amlak overthrew it at the Battle of Ansata in 1270, inaugurating the Solomonic dynasty. Under Emperor Amda Seyon I (r. 1314 to 1344) the empire expanded against neighbouring Muslim territories, and the Ethiopian-Adal War (1529 to 1543) weakened it.

Under Emperor Menelik II, Ethiopia defeated an Italian invasion at the Battle of Adwa in 1896 and remained independent during the Scramble for Africa. Italy invaded in 1936, and the country was liberated by the British Army in 1941; full sovereignty was restored in 1944. The Derg, a military junta, took power in 1974 after deposing Emperor Haile Selassie and ruled for nearly 17 years. Ethiopia is now a federal parliamentary republic.

It is a multi-ethnic state with more than 80 ethnic groups, of which the Oromo, Amhara, Somali and Tigrayans are the four largest. The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church is the largest denomination of Christianity, the most widely professed faith. Its capital, Addis Ababa, hosts the headquarters of the African Union Commission.
europe: Europe covers approximately 10,186,000 square kilometres, or 2% of Earth's surface, which makes it the second-smallest continent in the seven-continent model. It is commonly considered to be separated from Asia by the watershed of the Ural Mountains, the Ural River, the Caspian Sea, the Greater Caucasus, the Black Sea and the Turkish straits.

This eastern boundary is somewhat arbitrary and inconsistent compared with any clear-cut definition of a continent, and before it was adopted the border had been redefined several times as a series of rivers, seas and straits. Europe has a higher ratio of coast to landmass than any other continent, and warm Atlantic currents such as the Gulf Stream give much of it a temperate climate.

The earliest hominin discovered in Europe is Homo erectus georgicus, which lived roughly 1.8 million years ago in Georgia. Neanderthals appeared about 150,000 years ago and disappeared from the fossil record about 40,000 years ago, with the Iberian Peninsula as their final refuge. Modern humans seem to have appeared around 43,000 to 40,000 years ago, though there is evidence that Homo sapiens arrived around 54,000 years ago.

The culture of Europe takes ancient Greece and ancient Rome as crucial shared roots, particularly through their Christian successors. The fall of the Western Roman Empire in 476 CE and the Christian consolidation of Europe after the Migration Period marked the Middle Ages.

The Italian Renaissance spread across Western Europe, and from the Age of Discovery, led by Spain and Portugal, European powers colonised the Americas, almost all of Africa and Oceania, and the majority of Asia between the 16th and 20th centuries. The Industrial Revolution began in Great Britain at the end of the 18th century. Both world wars began and were fought to a great extent in Europe, and the Cold War divided the continent along the Iron Curtain until the Revolutions of 1989.

Europe had a total population of about 745 million in 2021, roughly a tenth of the world's people, and is politically divided into about fifty sovereign states. Russia is the largest and most populous, spanning 39% of the continent. The political map derives largely from the reorganisation after the Napoleonic Wars in 1815, and parliamentary democracy is now the prevalent form of government.
European integration has advanced since the founding of the Council of Europe in 1949, and the European Union, a supranational entity with 27 member states, represents the majority of the continent.
european-union: Visions of European unity existed well before the 19th century but gained ground as a reaction to the First World War. In 1920 John Maynard Keynes proposed a European customs union, and in 1923 the Paneuropean Union, the oldest organisation for European integration, was founded under Richard von Coudenhove-Kalergi. On 5 September 1929 Aristide Briand, Prime Minister of France, called in a speech at the League of Nations for a federal Europe to settle the historic Franco-German enmity. By the end of the following world war integration was seen as an antidote to the extreme nationalism that had caused it, and on 19 September 1946 Winston Churchill, speaking at the University of Zürich, repeated his calls for a European Union and a Council of Europe.

The Union's beginnings are traced to the Inner Six states, Belgium, France, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and West Germany, at the start of modern European integration in 1948. Treaties created the Western Union, the International Authority for the Ruhr, the European Coal and Steel Community, the European Economic Community and the European Atomic Energy Community, which increasingly merged. In 1969 a single currency became an official objective.

The European Union was established, along with its citizenship, when the Maastricht Treaty came into force in 1993, and the Treaty of Lisbon gave it a single international legal personality in 2009. It grew through the accession of 22 further states from 1973 to 2013. The flag of 12 golden stars on blue was designed in 1955 for the Council of Europe and adopted by the European Communities in 1986. In 2020 the United Kingdom became the only member state to leave.

The Union combines supranational and intergovernmental decision-making. It acts only within the competences the treaties give it, and only where the member states acting alone cannot achieve an objective. Regulations are enforceable at once in every member state, while directives must be put into national law. A country joining must meet the Copenhagen criteria set in 1993: a stable democracy that respects human rights and the rule of law, a functioning market economy and acceptance of EU law. The internal market rests on the free movement of people, goods, services and capital, and passport controls have been abolished within the Schengen Area. The Union was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2012.
